**AMAT model vs measurement** (mean absolute % error over the whole sweep): 4k: 6.4%, large: 8.3%

DRAM latency with 4 KB pages exceeds huge pages by **19.1 ns** (21%): page-walk cost folded into 'memory latency'.

**Prefetching (sequential chase) at the largest working set:** stride 64 B: 4.4 ns, stride 256 B: 4.8 ns, stride 1024 B: 9.4 ns; random: 110.0 ns.

## 4. Access intensity, the knee, and Little's Law

**Single core (independent random chains, 1 GiB):** idle latency 91.7 ns, peak 11.80 GB/s. Little's Law, L = λ·W: in-flight lines = 11.80 GB/s / 64 B x 91.7 ns = **16.9**, an estimate of the core's outstanding-miss limit (L1 fill buffers / superqueue). Latency per hop exceeds 1.25x idle at **16 chains**.

On AMD, `llc_ref` = L2 misses (requests that reach the L3, AMD's LLC), `llc_miss` = demand fills from DRAM, `dtlb_miss` = L2 DTLB misses (page walks). Event mapping: analysis/uprof_events.csv._

**Runtime vs counters (least squares, per element, all kernel runs):** ns/elem = a + b1·L1-miss/elem + b2·LLC-miss/elem + b3·dTLB-miss/elem. The coefficients are AMAT-style effective miss penalties (overlapped by prefetching/MLP, so far below the idle latencies).

At 262144 pages, 4 KB pages cost **22.7 ns more per access** than huge pages. With 1.03 dTLB misses/access that is ~22 ns per miss (page walk). At 16 pages (inside TLB reach) the difference is -0.0 ns: huge pages do not help when the TLB already covers the footprint.
